warmup.q: The makers of Quarkus, a framework for Java services, measured one service on a normal JVM and as a native image. The native image answered its first request in 581 ms instead of 4,417 ms. What happened to the most requests per second it could handle once busy?
options: It went up, because all the code was compiled before the program ran
It can't be measured, because native images have no JIT
warmup.why: Native peak throughput was 5,411 requests per second against 13,265 on the JVM. Code compiled ahead of time is compiled without the profiles a JIT gathers from the real run, so it's less specialized. Native wins start-up and memory (95 MiB against 304 MiB of RSS), not peak speed. Profile-guided optimization helps, but only in Oracle GraalVM. The first section has the whole table.

opening:
Even with a full back room, the shop has a morning routine: wheel out the shelves, switch on the tills, get up to speed. Now picture a pop-up stall, built at a factory, fully stocked and loaded onto a van. Park it, open the shutter, and you're trading at once. The catch is printed on the side: it sells only what the factory packed.

GraalVM's native image builds that stall. It turns your program, and the parts of the JDK it uses, into one ready-to-run file, with no JVM to start. Lesson 2's AOT cache still left a JVM that interprets first and compiles later; a native image does all of that in the build.

The trap is the customer who asks for something by name, from a note in their pocket. Code that picks a class by a name it reads at run time works on every JVM, and fails in a native image. In this lesson, we'll see what the build packs, list what it can't see, catch code that runs at the factory, and meet Quarkus, a framework that writes the list for you. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a pop-up stall packed at a factory, which opens at once and sells only what was packed. A native image is built the same way, from every call it can follow from main. Anything your code finds by name needs an entry on the list, and anything an initializer computes keeps the factory's value forever.

Now search your code for Class.forName(, getMethod(, newProxyInstance, and static final fields set from the clock or a random number. Each is a question the native build will ask.

Next, we'll keep the full JVM and skip the warm-up instead. What does CRaC save when it photographs a running JVM, and what must let go before the camera clicks?

sections.h: Native image builds a closed world
sections.html:
Lesson 2's best result still started a JVM. Even with a perfect AOT cache, the JVM maps its classes, links what training missed, interprets, and waits for the JIT. In a benchmark that the Quarkus project publishes for one of its sample services, the first request still took 1,859 ms with the cache. (Quarkus is a framework for Java services, and we'll meet it properly in the last section.) Native image removes that work from every start by doing it once, in the build.

The tool is called native-image. It comes with GraalVM, a JDK from Oracle with extra tools, or with Mandrel, a build of the same tool that the Quarkus project tailors for its framework. A plain OpenJDK doesn't have it. GraalVM comes in two editions, the open-source Community Edition and Oracle GraalVM, and the difference matters below. native-image takes your class path and builds one executable file for one operating system and one kind of CPU, in three steps.

First it analyzes the program. Starting at main, it follows every method call and field access it can see, and works out which classes can show up at each call. Second, it runs static initializers where it can. It saves the objects they create into the image heap, a part of the executable that is mapped straight into memory at start-up. Third, it compiles every method it reached to machine code.

Code the analysis never reached is left out, and so are the JDK classes nothing uses. That's the closed-world assumption: everything the program will ever run is known when you build it. In the shop picture, the factory packs the stall by following the shop's own catalogue. Every item a page points to goes in the van, and nothing else does.

The finished binary runs on a small runtime called Substrate VM, with no class loading, no bytecode verification, no interpreter and no JIT. That's why it starts in milliseconds and stays small. The Quarkus benchmark (Quarkus 3.34.3 on JDK 25.0.2, tuned by its authors) puts numbers on it:

JVM JVM + AOT cache Native image (Mandrel)
Time to first request 4,417 ms 1,859 ms 581 ms
Peak throughput 13,265 requests/s 12,389 requests/s 5,411 requests/s
RSS 304 MiB 240 MiB 95 MiB
Build about 30 s build plus a training run 3 to 10 min, 4 to 8 GB of RAM

Peak throughput, the most requests per second a service handles once it's busy, is 59% lower as a native image. With no JIT, there are no profiles from the real run. GraalVM's own docs say that "without profiling information, it is difficult to generate machine code of the same quality as a JIT compiler". The stall's staff follow a printed script, and they never learn shortcuts. Profile-guided optimization (PGO), building again with profiles recorded from a test run, narrows the gap, but "PGO is not available in GraalVM Community Edition", only in Oracle GraalVM. The default garbage collector is Serial, a single-threaded collector "optimized for low footprint and small Java heap sizes". G1 is available only in Oracle GraalVM, on Linux.

The other price is everything the analysis can't see. Reflection is code that looks up classes and methods by name while it runs. The analysis can't follow reflection, and it can't follow dynamic proxies, resources (files packed in a JAR) loaded by name, JNI (calls into native C code) or serialization (turning objects into bytes and back) either. The analysis is clever, not psychic. It works out reflective calls at build time "given that all the call arguments are constant", so Class.forName("tracker.ParcelScanned"), with the name written in the code, just works.

The tracking service isn't that lucky. It reads messages from its depots, and each message names its event class in a header: Class.forName(message.header("type")). The build can't know that name. You have to tell it, or the call fails at run time. Current GraalVM throws MissingReflectionRegistrationError, which "extends java.lang.Error and should not be handled".

Here the stall picture breaks, and the break costs real time. Changing one price tag on a real stall takes a minute. Changing one line of your code means building the whole stall again at the factory, which takes minutes and gigabytes of memory, every time.

A native image runs only what the build could see. Anything your code finds by name must be on a list.

GraalVM calls that list reachability metadata, and the next section writes one.

try.title: A class name that only exists at run time
steps: Read DynamicLookupDemo. It calls a static method with no arguments, chosen by two strings.
Run it as it is, then with -Pargs='java.util.UUID randomUUID'. On the JVM, any class on the class path works.
Ask yourself which classes a build would have to keep to support every possible argument. That's why the build needs a list.

Optional, with a GraalVM JDK: run the class with java -agentlib:native-image-agent=config-output-dir=build/ni -cp startup/build/classes/java/demo workbench.startup.l03.demo.DynamicLookupDemo java.util.UUID randomUUID, and read the JSON the agent wrote into build/ni.

code.title: DynamicLookupDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.startup.l03.demo; import java.lang.reflect.Method; /** * Calls a static, no-argument method chosen at run time, by class name and method name. * On the JVM any class on the class path works. A native image can only do this for the * classes and methods listed in its reachability metadata, so the demo prints that entry too. */ public class DynamicLookupDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String className = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "java.time.LocalDate"; String methodName = args.length > 1 ? args[1] : "now"; Class<?> type = Class.forName(className); // a name from data: the analysis can't see it Method method = type.getMethod(methodName); System.out.println(className + "." + methodName + "() = " + method.invoke(null)); System.out.println("A native image needs this in reachability-metadata.json:"); System.out.printf("{ \"reflection\": [ { \"type\": \"%s\", \"methods\": [ { \"name\": \"%s\", \"parameterTypes\": [] } ] } ] }%n", type.getName(), method.getName()); } }

alt.title: DynamicLookupDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.startup.l03.demo /** * Calls a static, no-argument method chosen at run time, by class name and method name. * On the JVM any class on the class path works. A native image can only do this for the * classes and methods listed in its reachability metadata, so the demo prints that entry too. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val className = args.getOrElse(0) { "java.time.LocalDate" } val methodName = args.getOrElse(1) { "now" } val type = Class.forName(className) // a name from data: the analysis can't see it val method = type.getMethod(methodName) println("$className.$methodName() = ${method.invoke(null)}") println("A native image needs this in reachability-metadata.json:") println("""{ "reflection": [ { "type": "${type.name}", "methods": [ { "name": "${method.name}", "parameterTypes": [] } ] } ] }""") }

try.expect: The first run prints today's date, such as java.time.LocalDate.now() = 2026-11-17, and the entry { "reflection": [ { "type": "java.time.LocalDate", "methods": [ { "name": "now", "parameterTypes": [] } ] } ] }. The second prints a random UUID and the same entry for java.util.UUID and randomUUID. On the JVM both just work. A native image would work only for the class and method its metadata listed.

aside.title: Isn't this what Leyden does?
aside.html: No, although both work ahead of time. Leyden's AOT cache is an optimization for the normal JVM: the same JVM, with the same open world, and if the cache doesn't fit, the JVM simply runs without it. A native image is a different runtime with a closed world: no class loading, no JIT, and no way to run a class the build didn't see. JEP 544, in development for JDK 28, will put compiled code in the AOT cache while the JVM keeps its JIT. The two keep borrowing each other's strengths, but they make opposite promises.

video.title: Native image builds a closed world: only code reachable from main gets in, so a class named at run time needs a metadata entry

sections.h: Reflection and proxies need reachability metadata
sections.html:
You tell the build in a file named reachability-metadata.json, in the folder META-INF/native-image/<groupId>/<artifactId>/ on the class path. (A group id and an artifact id are the two names that identify a library, such as com.example and tracker.) The current schema, version 1.2.0, allows four keys at the top level: reflection, resources, foreign and comment. Proxies, serialization and JNI all live inside reflection entries. In the shop, this file is the packing list for the items customers ask for by name.

A reflection entry names a type, and the members your code uses on it:

{
  "reflection": [
    {
      "condition": { "typeReached": "tracker.EventDecoder" },
      "type": "tracker.ParcelScanned",
      "methods": [
        { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] },
        { "name": "parcelId", "parameterTypes": [] }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

A constructor is named <init>, the JVM's own name for it. Parameter types are fully qualified, primitives go by name (long, int), and every method needs parameterTypes, even an empty one. Instead of listing members, you can set allDeclaredConstructors or allPublicMethods, which keeps more code in the binary. The optional condition switches the entry on only once EventDecoder is reached at run time, which means just before its static initializer starts. Writing EventDecoder.class on its own doesn't count.

A dynamic proxy is an object the JDK builds while the program runs: it implements a list of interfaces and sends every call to one handler method. Web client libraries use them a lot. The tracking service's DepotClient, which asks a depot where a parcel is, is one. In the metadata, a proxy is a reflection entry whose type is the ordered list of its interfaces:

{ "reflection": [ { "type": { "proxy": ["tracker.DepotClient", "java.lang.AutoCloseable"] } } ] }

The order is part of the proxy's identity: a proxy for (A, B) is a different class from one for (B, A), as the Try it below shows. If the proxy gets serialized, add "serializable": true; the docs say proxies "can only be registered for serialization via the JSON files".

Two warnings about what you'll find online. The older schema, v1.1.0, had separate top-level jni and serialization sections, and some GraalVM pages still show a top-level jni array, which v1.2.0 rejects. The current Quarkus development docs tell you to use "a proxy section", which v1.2.0 rejects too. Check your file against the schema of the GraalVM you build with.

You rarely write all of it by hand. The tracing agent watches a run on a normal JVM and writes down every reflective call it saw:

java -agentlib:native-image-agent=config-output-dir=build/ni-config -jar tracker.jar

Like an AOT training run, the agent sees only the code paths you exercise, so drive it with real tests, then read what it wrote. To make a missing entry fail loudly, build with --exact-reachability-metadata, and run your tests with -XX:MissingRegistrationReportingMode=Exit.

Write the list from what the code really does, then let a test prove it's complete.

The list covers what the analysis can't see. But the factory also runs some of your code while it builds, and that has a surprise of its own.

try.title: The order of proxy interfaces
steps: Read ProxyOrderDemo. It builds three proxies: (DepotApi, AutoCloseable), (AutoCloseable, DepotApi), and the first pair again.
Predict the two same class lines before you run it.
Run it, then the Kotlin twin.

code.title: ProxyOrderDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.startup.l03.demo; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.Arrays; /** Builds two JDK dynamic proxies from the same two interfaces, in opposite orders. */ public class ProxyOrderDemo { public interface DepotApi { String locate(String parcelId); } public static void main(String[] args) { InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, a) -> method.getName().equals("locate") ? "OUT FOR DELIVERY " + a[0] : null; ClassLoader loader = ProxyOrderDemo.class.getClassLoader(); Object first = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[] {DepotApi.class, AutoCloseable.class}, handler); Object second = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[] {AutoCloseable.class, DepotApi.class}, handler); Object again = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[] {DepotApi.class, AutoCloseable.class}, handler); System.out.println("first : " + first.getClass().getName() + " " + names(first.getClass())); System.out.println("second: " + second.getClass().getName() + " " + names(second.getClass())); System.out.println("same class for (A, B) and (B, A)? " + (first.getClass() == second.getClass())); System.out.println("same class for (A, B) twice? " + (first.getClass() == again.getClass())); System.out.println(((DepotApi) first).locate("PX-1042")); } static String names(Class<?> c) { return Arrays.toString(Arrays.stream(c.getInterfaces()).map(Class::getSimpleName).toArray()); } }

alt.title: ProxyOrderDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.startup.l03.demo import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler import java.lang.reflect.Proxy /** Builds two JDK dynamic proxies from the same two interfaces, in opposite orders. */ interface DepotApi { fun locate(parcelId: String): String } fun main() { val handler = InvocationHandler { _, method, a -> if (method.name == "locate") "OUT FOR DELIVERY ${a[0]}" else null } val loader = DepotApi::class.java.classLoader val first = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, arrayOf(DepotApi::class.java, AutoCloseable::class.java), handler) val second = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, arrayOf(AutoCloseable::class.java, DepotApi::class.java), handler) val again = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, arrayOf(DepotApi::class.java, AutoCloseable::class.java), handler) fun names(c: Class<*>) = c.interfaces.map { it.simpleName } println("first : ${first.javaClass.name} ${names(first.javaClass)}") println("second: ${second.javaClass.name} ${names(second.javaClass)}") println("same class for (A, B) and (B, A)? ${first.javaClass == second.javaClass}") println("same class for (A, B) twice? ${first.javaClass == again.javaClass}") println((first as DepotApi).locate("PX-1042")) }

try.expect: The first two proxies are different classes, jdk.proxy1.$Proxy0 and jdk.proxy1.$Proxy1, so same class for (A, B) and (B, A)? prints false. The repeat of the first pair reuses $Proxy0 and prints true, and the last line is OUT FOR DELIVERY PX-1042. The JVM keeps one proxy class per ordered list of interfaces, which is why the metadata lists them in order.

sections.h: The build is your program's first run
sections.html:
Class initialization is the other half of the story. GraalVM's docs give the numbers: "the simple 'Hello, World!' application requires more than 300 classes to be initialized". In code compiled ahead of time, checking "is this class initialized yet?" on every access "can reduce performance by more than twofold". So the builder runs static initializers at build time wherever it can, and stores what they produced in the image heap. The stall's displays are built at the factory.

Plain GraalVM initializes most JDK classes at build time, and your own classes only when it can prove that's safe. An initializer that calls native code (System.out.println counts) or makes a call it can't pin to one target stays at run time. Quarkus goes further: "By default, Quarkus initializes all classes at build time."

So your static initializer runs on the build machine, once, and its results are frozen into the binary:

Java
static final Instant STARTED_AT = Instant.now();   // the build's clock, on every start
static final Random JITTER = new Random();         // the builder refuses this one
Kotlin
val startedAt: Instant = Instant.now()             // the build's clock, on every start
val jitter = Random()                              // the builder refuses this one

These two lines come from BuildTimeInitDemo, in the Try it below. The second one is a retry jitter: a small random delay before trying again, so that many copies of a service don't all retry at the same moment. On a JVM, each run prints a new start time and a new delay. In a native image with build-time initialization, STARTED_AT would tell every user, for months, the moment the factory built the stall.

The builder catches some of these. Quarkus lists two errors you're likely to meet: "Detected an instance of Random/SplittableRandom class in the image heap. Instances created during image generation have cached seed values", and "No instances are allowed in the image heap for a class that is initialized or reinitialized at image runtime: sun.security.provider.NativePRNG". A seed is the starting value of a random number generator, and the same seed gives the same "random" numbers. Don't count on the builder for anything else. A timestamp, the computer's name, a token fetched at start: whatever an initializer computes, every copy started from that binary sees the build's value.

The fix is to initialize that class at run time instead:

quarkus.native.additional-build-args=--initialize-at-run-time=tracker.InstanceInfo\\,tracker.RetryJitter

Quarkus needs the comma escaped like that. With plain native-image, the options are --initialize-at-run-time= and --initialize-at-build-time=, and -H:+PrintClassInitialization reports which classes were initialized where. Better still, keep per-copy values out of static initializers altogether, and compute them in a method that runs when the program starts.

Whatever a static initializer computes, the build computes once. Keep per-run values out of it.

Writing these lists by hand is fine for one decoder. For a whole service, you'd want the framework to write them for you.

try.title: Values that would be frozen at build time
steps: Read BuildTimeInitDemo. Two static fields are set in a class initializer.
Run it twice and compare the two outputs.
Now imagine the class was initialized at build time, the Quarkus default. Which line would be the same on every start of every copy, and which one would stop the build?

code.title: BuildTimeInitDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.startup.l03.demo; import java.time.Instant; import java.util.Random; /** * Static state computed in a class initializer. On the JVM it is computed again on every start. * In a native image built with build-time initialization (the Quarkus default), the initializer * runs once, inside the build, and every start of the binary sees the build's values. */ public class BuildTimeInitDemo { static final class InstanceInfo { static final Instant STARTED_AT = Instant.now(); // build-time init: the build's time, forever static final Random JITTER = new Random(); // build-time init: the native builder rejects it } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("started at: " + InstanceInfo.STARTED_AT); System.out.println("retry jitter ms: " + InstanceInfo.JITTER.nextInt(250)); } }

alt.title: BuildTimeInitDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.startup.l03.demo import java.time.Instant import java.util.Random /** * Static state computed in a class initializer. On the JVM it is computed again on every start. * In a native image built with build-time initialization (the Quarkus default), the initializer * runs once, inside the build, and every start of the binary sees the build's values. */ object InstanceInfo { val startedAt: Instant = Instant.now() // build-time init: the build's time, forever val jitter = Random() // build-time init: the native builder rejects it } fun main() { println("started at: ${InstanceInfo.startedAt}") println("retry jitter ms: ${InstanceInfo.jitter.nextInt(250)}") }

try.expect: On the JVM each run prints a new started at time and a new jitter value, because the initializer runs at every start: one run printed started at: 2026-11-17T07:11:25.498913321Z and retry jitter ms: 148. Initialized at build time, started at would print the build's moment forever, in every copy. The Random in the image heap is one of the cases the builder refuses, with the "cached seed values" error.

sections.h: Quarkus writes most of the metadata for you
sections.html:
Quarkus is an open-source framework for writing services in Java and Kotlin, and it's the second half of this lesson's title. Its main idea is the one this track keeps coming back to: do at build time what other frameworks do at every start. It scans and wires your program while it builds, and it treats native image as a first-class target, which it calls Quarkus native.

Quarkus is made of extensions, add-on modules that each bring one library, such as a JSON library or a database driver. Each extension knows what its library reflects on, and Quarkus generates reachability-metadata.json itself. Your part is the classes only your own code knows about, and you declare them with annotations:

Java
@RegisterForReflection
public record ParcelScanned(String parcelId, String depot, long weightGrams) { }

@RegisterForReflection(targets = {DepotReply.class, DepotError.class})   // a library's classes
public class DepotReflectionConfig { }

@RegisterForProxy(targets = {DepotClient.class, AutoCloseable.class})    // order matters
public class DepotProxyConfig { }
Kotlin
@RegisterForReflection
data class ParcelScanned(val parcelId: String, val depot: String, val weightGrams: Long)

@RegisterForReflection(targets = [DepotReply::class, DepotError::class])  // a library's classes
class DepotReflectionConfig

@RegisterForProxy(targets = [DepotClient::class, AutoCloseable::class])   // order matters
class DepotProxyConfig

@RegisterForReflection registers methods and fields by default, plus any nested classes unless you set ignoreNested = true. With targets, it registers the listed classes and not the class it sits on, which is how you cover a library's classes that you can't annotate. serialization = true adds Java serialization. @RegisterForProxy takes the interfaces in order, and the Quarkus docs repeat that "the order of the specified proxy interfaces is significant". Resources go in application.properties, Quarkus's settings file: quarkus.native.resources.includes=templates/**,postcodes/*.csv.

When you do need JSON, put it in src/main/resources/META-INF/native-image/<group-id>/<artifact-id>/. The current docs warn that Quarkus overwrites a file placed directly in META-INF/native-image/. Versions matter here too. The latest 3.x release is 3.40.1.1, and its guides still show the older separate files, reflect-config.json and proxy-config.json, while the 4.0 guides say those legacy files "are not supported". Write the unified reachability-metadata.json, and the file survives the upgrade.

./mvnw verify -Dnative (mvnw runs Maven, a build tool) builds the binary and runs your integration tests against it. Integration tests start the whole program and talk to it from outside. Because a native build takes minutes and gigabytes, most teams build it in a shared build, not after every change, and develop in JVM mode. Quarkus's own advice is "Start with JVM mode. Move to native when you have a concrete need." Lesson 4 of this track turns that into a decision table.

Check before the lab: your scan events live in a shared JAR that another team owns, so you can't annotate them. Which annotation do you add, and on which class? (@RegisterForReflection(targets = {...}) on any class in your own code, listing their classes. The class carrying the annotation isn't registered itself.)

A native image wins the start and the memory, and pays at peak speed and in the build. The next lesson keeps the full JVM, JIT and all, and skips the warm-up instead.

java.html: @RegisterForReflection public record ParcelScanned(String parcelId, String depot, long weightGrams) { } // the same thing by hand in reachability-metadata.json: // { "type": "tracker.ParcelScanned", // "methods": [ // { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] }, // { "name": "parcelId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] }

kotlin.title: ParcelScanned.kt
kotlin.html: @RegisterForReflection data class ParcelScanned(val parcelId: String, val depot: String, val weightGrams: Long) // the same thing by hand: the accessor is a getter on the JVM // { "type": "tracker.ParcelScanned", // "methods": [ // { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] }, // { "name": "getParcelId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] }

compare.note: The annotation is the same, and Quarkus reads it the same way from both languages. What differs is the bytecode it describes. A Java record has an accessor named parcelId(). A Kotlin val parcelId compiles to a private field and a method named getParcelId(). Hand-written metadata names JVM members, so the two entries differ even though the sources look alike. A non-null Kotlin Long is the primitive long in the constructor's signature; Long? would be java.lang.Long. Annotation arrays are {...} with .class in Java and [...] with ::class in Kotlin.

worked.title: Write the metadata for a scan decoder

steps.say: Here is the tracking service's decoder: each message from a depot names its event class in a header. Find every reflective call and, for each one, the exact member it needs. Ignore code that names a class in the source, such as new or a direct method call: the analysis sees those.
steps.code: Object decode(Message msg) throws ReflectiveOperationException { Class<?> type = Class.forName(msg.header("type")); // 1 Object event = type.getConstructor(String.class, String.class, long.class) // 2 .newInstance(msg.parcelId(), msg.depot(), msg.weightGrams()); log.info(type.getMethod("parcelId").invoke(event)); // 3 return event; }

alt.html: fun decode(msg: Message): Any { val type = Class.forName(msg.header("type")) // 1 val event = type.getConstructor(String::class.java, String::class.java, Long::class.javaPrimitiveType) // 2 .newInstance(msg.parcelId(), msg.depot(), msg.weightGrams()) log.info(type.getMethod("parcelId").invoke(event)) // 3 return event }

steps.say: There are three needs: (1) the class by name, for every event type a depot can send; (2) its (String, String, long) constructor; (3) its parcelId() method. Say the depots send ParcelScanned and ParcelDelivered. Each gets one entry, and the condition limits them to binaries where the decoder is used.
steps.code: { "reflection": [ { "condition": { "typeReached": "tracker.EventDecoder" }, "type": "tracker.ParcelScanned", "methods": [ { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] }, { "name": "parcelId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] }, { "condition": { "typeReached": "tracker.EventDecoder" }, "type": "tracker.ParcelDelivered", "methods": [ { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] }, { "name": "parcelId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] } ] }

steps.say: Put the file at src/main/resources/META-INF/native-image/com.example/tracker/reachability-metadata.json, the <groupId>/<artifactId> folder. In a Quarkus service, the annotation does the same job, and it moves with the class when someone renames it. That's the version to prefer.
steps.code: @RegisterForReflection public record ParcelScanned(String parcelId, String depot, long weightGrams) { } @RegisterForReflection public record ParcelDelivered(String parcelId, String depot, long weightGrams) { }

alt.html: @RegisterForReflection data class ParcelScanned(val parcelId: String, val depot: String, val weightGrams: Long) @RegisterForReflection data class ParcelDelivered(val parcelId: String, val depot: String, val weightGrams: Long)

steps.say: Prove it in the shared build. Build the native binary and run the integration tests against it, with missing registrations turned into a hard exit. A new event type that nobody registered now fails the build, not a parcel at three in the morning.
steps.code: ./mvnw verify -Dnative \ -Dquarkus.native.additional-build-args=--exact-reachability-metadata # and start the binary under test with -XX:MissingRegistrationReportingMode=Exit

lab.title: Write reachability metadata for a class and a proxy
steps: Run the tests once. Eight of the ten fail. Two MetadataFileTest checks pass already, because the empty file you start with has a valid shape.
Read EventDecoder and DepotClients. Write down every reflective call: which class, which constructor (with its parameter types), which methods, and which proxy interfaces in which order.

Edit reachability-metadata.json by hand. Add one reflection entry for workbench.startup.l03.ParcelScanned with its <init> and the three accessors from EventDecoder.ACCESSORS, and one entry whose type is {"proxy": [...]}. Run MetadataFileTest until it passes.
Implement MetadataWriter.reflection and MetadataWriter.proxy, so the same entries can be generated from Class objects. Run all ten tests.
hints: A method entry needs both keys, even with no parameters: {"name": "depot", "parameterTypes": []}.
Class.getName() gives exactly the names the schema wants: java.lang.String for a class, long for a primitive.
m instanceof Constructor<?> tells a constructor from a method. Class.isInterface() and a HashSet cover the two proxy rules.
lab.done: All ten tests in MetadataFileTest and MetadataWriterTest pass.

drill.title: Two entries from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a reachability-metadata.json that registers (1) a JDK proxy over com.example.library.CatalogClient and java.io.Closeable, in that order, and (2) the (java.lang.String, long) constructor of com.example.library.Loan, active only once com.example.library.LoanListener is reached. Then check: how many top-level keys did you use?

answer.html: { "reflection": [ { "type": { "proxy": ["com.example.library.CatalogClient", "java.io.Closeable"] } }, { "condition": { "typeReached": "com.example.library.LoanListener" }, "type": "com.example.library.Loan", "methods": [ { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "long"] } ] } ] }

recap: Native image (GraalVM or Mandrel; a plain OpenJDK can't build one) analyzes the program from main and keeps only reachable code. It starts in milliseconds with a small RSS, but has no JIT, so peak throughput is lower (59% lower in Quarkus's benchmark), and builds take minutes and gigabytes.
Whatever the analysis can't see (reflection by a run-time name, proxies, resources, JNI, serialization) must be listed in META-INF/native-image/<groupId>/<artifactId>/reachability-metadata.json.
Schema v1.2.0 has only reflection, resources, foreign and comment at the top. A proxy is a reflection entry with "type": {"proxy": [interfaces in order]}, and a constructor is <init>.
The build runs static initializers, and Quarkus does it for all classes by default: their values are frozen into the binary. Use --initialize-at-run-time, or compute per-copy values at start-up.
In Quarkus, prefer @RegisterForReflection (with targets for a library's classes) and @RegisterForProxy to hand-written JSON, and test the native binary in your shared build.
The limit: a native image can never run a class the build didn't see, and it gives up the JIT's peak speed. Keeping the full JVM while skipping warm-up needs another tool, the next lesson's.

explain.prompt: Explain to a friend why a native image needs metadata for the event class your decoder creates by reflection, but not for a class your code creates with new, and what Quarkus gives you so you don't write the JSON by hand.
explain.answer: The native build analyzes the program from main and keeps only code it can prove is reachable. A new ParcelScanned(...) is right there in the bytecode, so the analysis sees the class and its constructor. The decoder instead calls Class.forName with a name from the message header, then getConstructor and getMethod, so the build can't know which class or which members until the message arrives. Unless the class and those members are listed in reachability metadata, they're left out, and the call fails at run time with a registration error. In Quarkus, the extensions register what their libraries need, and I add @RegisterForReflection to my event classes, with targets for classes from a library, and @RegisterForProxy for proxies. Quarkus turns those into the metadata file during the build.

deeper.html:
Some details for when you go native for real.

Conditions are precise. "condition": {"typeReached": "tracker.EventDecoder"} makes an entry active when that type is reached at run time, which the docs define as "right before the class-initialization routine starts for that type", or when one of its subtypes is reached. Writing EventDecoder.class doesn't reach it. Conditions mostly help library authors ship metadata that costs nothing in programs that never use the feature.

Resources use globs: {"resources": [{"glob": "META-INF/**/*.properties"}, {"bundle": "tracker.Messages"}]}. In Quarkus, use quarkus.native.resources.includes instead.

The heap needs a limit. Without an explicit maximum, a native image sets the maximum Java heap to 80% of the physical memory, according to the GraalVM memory docs. In a container, pass -Xmx (or -XX:MaximumHeapSizePercent) yourself. The default collector is Serial. --gc=G1 needs Oracle GraalVM on Linux, and --gc=epsilon never frees memory, which only makes sense for short jobs.

PGO, in Oracle GraalVM only, is a three-step build: native-image --pgo-instrument ... builds an instrumented binary, you run it on a real workload so it writes a .iprof profile when it exits, and native-image --pgo=app.iprof ... builds the optimized binary. That's the same idea as Leyden's training run, applied to compiled code.

The JDK is moving toward some of these gains without leaving the JVM. Lesson 2's AOT cache already ships linked classes and profiles, and JEP 544, in development for JDK 28, adds compiled code to the cache while keeping the JIT. Native image stays the option when the binary's size and start time, not the JVM's, are the limit.
